title: Check if Numbers Are Ascending in a Sentence
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if all numbers appearing in the sentence are strictly increasing.
Idea: `areNumbersAscending` scans tokens, parses each numeric token, and compares it with the previous number, rejecting any value that is not strictly greater.
Technique and why it applies: Comparing each extracted number to the previous one verifies strict ascending order without sorting.
Invariant: `prev` stores the last extracted integer, so every new number must exceed all earlier numbers by transitivity of strict increase.
Edge cases: The sentence may contain no numbers, which is valid; equality is not ascending; numeric tokens are separated by spaces.
Complexity: O(n) time in sentence length and O(1) auxiliary space aside from token parsing.
complexity_reason: Comparing each extracted number to the previous one verifies strict ascending order without sorting.

title: Check if Numbers Are Ascending in a Sentence
notes:

Technique and why it applies: Comparing each extracted number to the previous one verifies strict ascending order without sorting.
Invariant: `prev` stores the last extracted integer, so every new number must exceed all earlier numbers by transitivity of strict increase.
Edge cases: The sentence may contain no numbers, which is valid; equality is not ascending; numeric tokens are separated by spaces.
Complexity: O(n) time in sentence length and O(1) auxiliary space aside from token parsing.
code: class Solution { public boolean areNumbersAscending(String s){String[]w=s.split(" ");int prev=-1;for(String x:w)if(!x.isEmpty()&&Character.isDigit(x.charAt(0))){int n=Integer.parseInt(x);if(n<=prev)return false;prev=n;}return true;} }
complexity_reason: Comparing each extracted number to the previous one verifies strict ascending order without sorting.

title: Kth Distinct String in an Array
approach_name: Scan distinct values in original order
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the kth string that occurs exactly once, or an empty string if fewer than k exist.
Idea: Count each string with a frequency map, then scan `arr` in original order and decrement `k` only for strings with frequency one.
Technique and why it applies: Frequency counting first identifies unique strings, while the original-order pass selects the kth one.
Invariant: The second pass preserves original order, and only values whose total frequency equals one consume a distinct rank.
Edge cases: If fewer than `k` distinct strings exist, return an empty string; repeated strings never count toward the rank.
Complexity: O(n·L) expected time and O(u·L) space for u distinct strings of average length L.
complexity_reason: Frequency counting first identifies unique strings, while the original-order pass selects the kth one.

title: Kth Distinct String in an Array
approach_name: Scan distinct values in original order
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the kth string that occurs exactly once, or an empty string if fewer than k exist.
Idea: Count each string with a frequency map, then scan `arr` in original order and decrement `k` only for strings with frequency one.
Technique and why it applies: Frequency counting first identifies unique strings, while the original-order pass selects the kth one.
Invariant: The second pass preserves original order, and only values whose total frequency equals one consume a distinct rank.
Edge cases: If fewer than `k` distinct strings exist, return an empty string; repeated strings never count toward the rank.
Complexity: O(n·L) expected time and O(u·L) space for u distinct strings of average length L.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public String kthDistinct(String[] arr,int k){Map<String,Integer>c=new HashMap<>();for(String s:arr)c.put(s,c.getOrDefault(s,0)+1);for(String s:arr)if(c.get(s)==1&&--k==0)return s;return "";} }
complexity_reason: Frequency counting first identifies unique strings, while the original-order pass selects the kth one.

title: Smallest Index With Equal Value
approach_name: Find first index matching value modulo ten
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the smallest i for which i modulo 10 equals nums[i], or -1.
Idea: Scan indices from left to right and return the first `i` satisfying `i % 10 == nums[i]`; return -1 if none qualifies.
Technique and why it applies: A left-to-right scan returns the earliest index satisfying the modulo-ten equality.
Invariant: Because indices are visited in increasing order, the first match is necessarily the smallest valid index.
Edge cases: The match is exact equality; index zero is a valid candidate; no match returns -1.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: A left-to-right scan returns the earliest index satisfying the modulo-ten equality.

title: Count Vowel Substrings of a String
notes:
Task and constraints: Count substrings consisting only of vowels and containing all five vowels.
Idea: For every starting position containing a vowel, extend the end while characters remain vowels and count each prefix window whose seen-vowel set contains all five vowels.
Technique and why it applies: Expanding each vowel-only start counts every substring that includes all five vowel types.
Invariant: The current window contains only vowels, and its set records which of `a,e,i,o,u` have appeared.
Edge cases: Stop extension at a consonant; a valid substring must contain all five vowels; overlapping substrings are counted separately.
Complexity: O(n²) worst-case time and O(1) auxiliary space for the five-vowel set.
complexity_reason: Expanding each vowel-only start counts every substring that includes all five vowel types.

title: Count Vowel Substrings of a String
notes:

Idea: For every starting position containing a vowel, extend the end while characters remain vowels and count each prefix window whose seen-vowel set contains all five vowels.
Technique and why it applies: Expanding each vowel-only start counts every substring that includes all five vowel types.
Invariant: The current window contains only vowels, and its set records which of `a,e,i,o,u` have appeared.
Edge cases: Stop extension at a consonant; a valid substring must contain all five vowels; overlapping substrings are counted separately.
Complexity: O(n²) worst-case time and O(1) auxiliary space for the five-vowel set.
code: class Solution { public int countVowelSubstrings(String word){int ans=0;for(int i=0;i<word.length();i++){boolean[]v=new boolean[5];int n=0;for(int j=i;j<word.length();j++){char c=word.charAt(j);int k="aeiou".indexOf(c);if(k<0)break;if(!v[k]){v[k]=true;n++;}if(n==5)ans++;}}return ans;} }
complexity_reason: Expanding each vowel-only start counts every substring that includes all five vowel types.

title: Time Needed to Buy Tickets
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the time until person k finishes buying tickets, with one ticket sold per turn in queue order.
Idea: Sum `min(tickets[i], tickets[k])` for indices `i <= k` and `min(tickets[i], tickets[k]-1)` for indices `i > k`.
Technique and why it applies: Counting each person's contribution up to the target's finish time avoids simulating the queue round by round.
Invariant: People before or at `k` can buy at most `tickets[k]` times before `k` finishes, while people after `k` get one fewer turn.
Edge cases: The target person's required tickets are positive; positions after `k` lose the final round because the queue stops when `k` finishes.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code:
class Solution:
 def timeRequiredToBuy(self,tickets,k):return sum(min(x,tickets[k]-(i>k)) for i,x in enumerate(tickets))
complexity_reason: Counting each person's contribution up to the target's finish time avoids simulating the queue round by round.

title: Time Needed to Buy Tickets
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the time until person k finishes buying tickets, with one ticket sold per turn in queue order.
Idea: Sum `min(tickets[i], tickets[k])` for indices `i <= k` and `min(tickets[i], tickets[k]-1)` for indices `i > k`.
Technique and why it applies: Counting each person's contribution up to the target's finish time avoids simulating the queue round by round.
Invariant: People before or at `k` can buy at most `tickets[k]` times before `k` finishes, while people after `k` get one fewer turn.
Edge cases: The target person's required tickets are positive; positions after `k` lose the final round because the queue stops when `k` finishes.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public int timeRequiredToBuy(int[] tickets,int k){int ans=0;for(int i=0;i<tickets.length;i++)ans+=Math.min(tickets[i],tickets[k]-(i>k?1:0));return ans;} }
complexity_reason: Counting each person's contribution up to the target's finish time avoids simulating the queue round by round.

title: Count Common Words With One Occurrence
notes:
Task and constraints: Count words that occur exactly once in each of two arrays.
Idea: Build frequency maps for `words1` and `words2`, then count words whose frequency is exactly one in both maps.
Technique and why it applies: Separate frequency counts enforce the exactly-once condition independently in both input arrays.
Invariant: Each word qualifies only when its count in each separate array equals one.
Edge cases: A word repeated in either array is excluded; duplicate qualifying entries cannot arise because a frequency-one word appears only once per array.
Complexity: O(n+m) expected time and O(u+v) space for distinct words in both arrays.
complexity_reason: Separate frequency counts enforce the exactly-once condition independently in both input arrays.

title: Count Common Words With One Occurrence
notes:
Task and constraints: Count words that occur exactly once in each of two arrays.
Idea: Build frequency maps for `words1` and `words2`, then count words whose frequency is exactly one in both maps.
Technique and why it applies: Separate frequency counts enforce the exactly-once condition independently in both input arrays.
Invariant: Each word qualifies only when its count in each separate array equals one.
Edge cases: A word repeated in either array is excluded; duplicate qualifying entries cannot arise because a frequency-one word appears only once per array.
Complexity: O(n+m) expected time and O(u+v) space for distinct words in both arrays.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public int countWords(String[] words1,String[] words2){Map<String,Integer>a=new HashMap<>(),b=new HashMap<>();for(String s:words1)a.put(s,a.getOrDefault(s,0)+1);for(String s:words2)b.put(s,b.getOrDefault(s,0)+1);int n=0;for(String s:a.keySet())if(a.get(s)==1&&b.getOrDefault(s,0)==1)n++;return n;} }
complexity_reason: Separate frequency counts enforce the exactly-once condition independently in both input arrays.

title: Finding 3-Digit Even Numbers
notes:
Task and constraints: Return all unique three-digit even numbers that can be formed from the given digits, sorted ascending.
Idea: Enumerate three distinct digit indices, require a nonzero hundreds digit and an even units digit, insert the resulting number into a set, then sort the unique results.
Technique and why it applies: Enumerating index triples respects digit multiplicities, while a set deduplicates numbers formed by repeated digit values.
Invariant: Each candidate uses three different positions from `digits`; the set removes duplicate numeric values formed from repeated digit values.
Edge cases: Leading zero is forbidden; the last digit must be even; repeated digits can be used only as many times as they occur in the input.
Complexity: O(d³ + r log r) time for d digits and r distinct results, with O(r) space.
complexity_reason: Enumerating index triples respects digit multiplicities, while a set deduplicates numbers formed by repeated digit values.

title: Finding 3-Digit Even Numbers
notes:
Task and constraints: Return all unique three-digit even numbers that can be formed from the given digits, sorted ascending.
Idea: Enumerate three distinct digit indices, require a nonzero hundreds digit and an even units digit, insert the resulting number into a set, then sort the unique results.
Technique and why it applies: Enumerating index triples respects digit multiplicities, while a set deduplicates numbers formed by repeated digit values.
Invariant: Each candidate uses three different positions from `digits`; the set removes duplicate numeric values formed from repeated digit values.
Edge cases: Leading zero is forbidden; the last digit must be even; repeated digits can be used only as many times as they occur in the input.
Complexity: O(d³ + r log r) time for d digits and r distinct results, with O(r) space.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public int[] findEvenNumbers(int[] digits){Set<Integer>out=new TreeSet<>();for(int i=0;i<digits.length;i++)for(int j=0;j<digits.length;j++)for(int k=0;k<digits.length;k++)if(i!=j&&i!=k&&j!=k&&digits[i]!=0&&digits[k]%2==0)out.add(digits[i]*100+digits[j]*10+digits[k]);return out.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray();} }
complexity_reason: Enumerating index triples respects digit multiplicities, while a set deduplicates numbers formed by repeated digit values.

title: Rings and Rods
notes:
Task and constraints: Count rods that contain at least one red, green, and blue ring.
Idea: Use a 10-by-3 boolean presence table or per-rod color set, mark each ring's color on its rod, and count rods with all three colors.
Technique and why it applies: Tracking color presence per rod makes the all-three-colors condition a direct final check.
Invariant: A rod qualifies only when its state records red, green, and blue at least once.
Edge cases: Multiple rings of the same color do not change qualification; rod labels range from 0 through 9; all three distinct colors are required.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space for ten rods and three colors.
complexity_reason: Tracking color presence per rod makes the all-three-colors condition a direct final check.

title: Rings and Rods
notes:
Task and constraints: Count rods that contain at least one red, green, and blue ring.
Idea: Use a 10-by-3 boolean presence table or per-rod color set, mark each ring's color on its rod, and count rods with all three colors.
Technique and why it applies: Tracking color presence per rod makes the all-three-colors condition a direct final check.
Invariant: A rod qualifies only when its state records red, green, and blue at least once.
Edge cases: Multiple rings of the same color do not change qualification; rod labels range from 0 through 9; all three distinct colors are required.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space for ten rods and three colors.
code: class Solution { public int countPoints(String rings){boolean[][]seen=new boolean[10][3];for(int i=0;i<rings.length();i+=2){int rod=rings.charAt(i+1)-'0',color=rings.charAt(i)=='R'?0:rings.charAt(i)=='G'?1:2;seen[rod][color]=true;}int ans=0;for(boolean[]r:seen)if(r[0]&&r[1]&&r[2])ans++;return ans;} }
complexity_reason: Tracking color presence per rod makes the all-three-colors condition a direct final check.

title: Maximum Number of Words Found in Sentences
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the maximum word count among the sentences.
Idea: Count the words in each sentence using whitespace splitting or space count plus one, and keep the maximum.
Technique and why it applies: Computing each sentence's word count and maintaining the maximum directly matches the requested statistic.
Invariant: `best` is the largest word count among sentences processed so far.
Edge cases: Each sentence is nonempty under constraints; multiple spaces may matter if using a split-based implementation rather than counting spaces.
Complexity: O(total sentence characters) time and O(L) temporary space if splitting creates tokens.
code:
class Solution:
 def mostWordsFound(self,sentences):return max(len(s.split()) for s in sentences)
complexity_reason: Computing each sentence's word count and maintaining the maximum directly matches the requested statistic.

title: A Number After a Double Reversal
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if reversing the digits twice restores the original number.
Idea: Return true when `num` is zero or does not end in zero; otherwise return false.
Technique and why it applies: Only a nonzero trailing zero changes the numeric value during the first reversal and makes double reversal fail.
Invariant: Reversing twice restores every positive integer except those whose trailing zeros are dropped by the first reversal.
Edge cases: Zero reverses to zero; any nonzero number ending in zero loses those zeros when reversed and cannot recover them.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) space.
code:
class Solution:
 def isSameAfterReversals(self,num):return num==0 or num%10!=0
complexity_reason: Only a nonzero trailing zero changes the numeric value during the first reversal and makes double reversal fail.
